newsitem.title: UK: Stg/mark up half a pfennig in Europe on rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Stg/mark up half a pfennig in Europe on rate hike.

text.p: Sterling gained half a pfennig to above 2.82 marks at midday in Europe after The Bank of England raised UK interest rates by 0.25 percent to 6.50 percent.
The pound was at 2.8255/65 marks at 1110 GMT compared to 2.8190/00 just before the announcement. Cable was at $1.6262/72 vs $1.6235/45.
"The rise is understandable and if they were going to raise rates it is best to do it early," said Nick Parsons, foreign exchange strategist at Banque Paribas.
"There hasn't been a heavy move to sterling yet because of the U.S. payrolls but we're in for an extremely busy afternoon."
Sterling/mark, which dropped about half a pfennig shortly before the announcement, bounced sharply from just below 2.83 marts on the news but stayed shy of its session high at 2.8270.
Some analysts said sterling could push through the four-and-a-half-year high of 2.8331 set on Wednesday and move up even further.
"We could well be testing the highs (for sterling) we saw earlier this year," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
This was the first time since the bank was nationalised in 1945 that it had changed interest rates without being instructed by the government, and analysts had expected the move.

The rate hike showed the central bank is keen to demonstrate its independance, they said, but questions remained as to what action would be taken later in the year. Much depends on the content of new finance minister Gordon Brown's budget, due early in July, said economists.
"The uncertainty was about the timing rather than whether there would be a rate rise," said Simon Knapp, international economist at BZW.
"They've got this rate rise out of the way, but the greater uncertainties about rates are towards the end of the year," he added.
For the near-term, the market would be focusing on U.S. non-farm payroll figures for May due at 1230 GMT, with analysts expecting a 219,000 rise during the month compared to a 142,000 rise in April.
